element é,4-a and all integrals over }, will be with respect to the volume element
Oea. Thus, in particular, in order that our results be independent of our choice of
abcd, the Lagrangian density must be a scalar density on M and the momentum 7
(defined below) must be a tensor density on >,. As previously noted in our discussion
of the Einstein Lagrangian, the introduction of esa could be avoided by incorpo-
rating the volume element into the definition of £, 7, and other quantities, but we
choose not to do so since this procedure is rather cumbersome.
   The next step in giving a Hamiltonian formulation is to define a configuration
space for the field by specifying what tensor field (or fields) q on $, physically
describes the instantaneous configuration of the field y. The space of possible
momenta of the field at a given configuration q then is taken to be the “cotangent
space,” V,', of the configuration space at q. Since the set of possible configurations

  The presence of constraints in our Hamiltonian formulations of Maxwell’s equa-
tions and Einstein’s equations indicates that we have not isolated the “true dynamical
degrees of freedom” in our choice of configuration space. Even though we already
have eliminated V and N and N, as dynamical variables, the constraints tell us that
our phase space still is “too large.” This, in turn, is directly related to the gauge
freedom present in our configuration variables A and han, respectively. In the Max-
well case, A and A — vx represent the same physical configuration. This suggests
that we should take our configuration space to be not simply the space of vector
potentials, Z, but the space of equivalence classes, A, of vector potentials, where
two vector potentials are equivalent if they differ only by a gauge transformation.
The“cotangent space” at A then would be the space of linear functions of variations
of A which depend only on the equivalence class. Thus, the momenta would be
represented by vector fields7 having the property that

“deparameterize” the theory by solving the constraint for this momentum. However,

not appear possible to find a choice of configuration space for general relativity such
that only the “true dynamical degrees of freedom” are present in its phase space. The
presence of the constraint (E.2.33) appears to be an unavoidable feature of the
Hamiltonian formulation of general relativity. This provides a serious obstacle to the
formulation of a quantum theory of gravitation by the canonical quantization ap-
proach (see chapter 14).
      Finally, we return to the issue of boundary terms in the Hamiltonian formulation.
Consider, first, the case of a closed universe, i.e., M = R x }, where 5 is compact.
Consider the region, U, of M bounded by two constant time hypersurfaces 2, and
5. Then the modified gravitational action Sg, equation (E.1.42), will receive bound-
ary contributions from =, and 32. However, these boundary terms will be canceled
by the contributions of the third term on the right-hand side of equation (E.2.28).
Note that the fourth term in equation (E.2.28) yields no boundary contributions since
n*V,n° is orthogonal to the normal, n°, to 2 and 2». In addition, the last term in
equation (E.2.32) makes no contribution since there is no spatial boundary. Thus,
in the case of a closed universe, our final answer for Hg is unchanged when all
boundary terms are reinserted. Note that because of equations (E.2.33) and (E.2.34),
the numerical value of Hg vanishes for every solution. This suggests that we should
define the total energy of a closed universe to be zero. In other words, it suggests
that there does not exist a nontrivial notion of total energy in a closed universe.
However, this argument is not conclusive, since one always can “parameterize” a
theory in the manner mentioned above so as to make its Hamiltonian vanish. If
general relativity could be “deparameterized,” a notion of total energy in a closed
universe could well emerge.

than that the induced metric be held fixed on a distant spatial boundary. This new
boundary condition requires the addition of further boundary terms into the grav-

and (E.2.32) now will contribute to Hg. Instead of keeping careful account of all

UNITS AND DIMENSIONS




Geometrized Units
  In this book, we have used “geometrized units,” where the gravitational constant
G, and speed of light c, are set equal to one. All quantities which in ordinary units
have dimension expressible in terms of length L, time T, and mass M, are given the
dimension of a power of length in geometrized units. Since    G = c = 1, all factors
involving G and c may be omitted from formulas, and, indeed this is why it is
convenient to use geometrized units in general relativity. However, if one wishes to
evaluate quantities in ordinary, “nongeometrized” units, the factors of G and c must
be reinserted. This is casily done as follows.
   In “nongeometrized” units, the dimension of c is L/T and the dimension of G/c?
is L/M. Hence, the “conversion factor” relative to geometrized units for a quantity
with dimension of time is c, while the conversion factor for a quantity with dimen-
sion of mass is G/c?. More generally, a quantity with dimension L”7"M? in ordinary
units has dimension L”*"*? in geometrized units and the conversion factor is
c"(G/c?). The dimensions and conversion factors for some frequently encountered
quantities are given in Table F.1.
   In order to convert a formula written in geometrized units to one which is valid
in nongeometrized units, one first must identify the nongeometrized dimension of all
quantities appearing in the equation. Then one simply obtains the conversion factor
for each quantity from Table F.1 or computes it by the above formula. If one then
multiplies each quantity appearing in the equation by its conversion factor, the
resulting equation will be valid in nongeometrized units.

Planck Units
   For calculations involving quantum effects in general relativity, it is natural to
employ Planck units where Å is set equal to 1 in addition to G = c = 1. In Planck
units, all quantities which in ordinary units have dimension expressible in terms of
L,T, and M now become dimensionless. In particular, all lengths are expressed as
dimensionless multiples of the Planck length, lp = (Gh/c*)'*. To convert a formula
valid in Planck units to one valid in ordinary units, we simply identify the non-
geometrized dimension of all quantities appearing in the equation. Then we multiply
each such quantity by its conversion factor, which equals its conversion factor for
